rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb sāʾa means to sadden; the faces are made the object of the verb.
rows.anchor: ساءه يسوؤه، أي: أحزنه، وذكرنا ذلك في مواضع

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Faces can stand for their people, whose grief, joy, glad tidings, or gloom appears on their faces.
rows.anchor: قال أبو علي: قال: {وجوهكم} على أن الوجوه مفعول {ليسوءوا}

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The common plural reading suits both sense and wording: the resurrected people cause the Israelites grief and enter the mosque in parallel.
rows.anchor: وهذه قراءة العامة (¬4)، وهي وفق المعنى واللفظ

rows.speaker: حمزة
rows.claim: Hamza reads the verb as singular, with yāʾ.
rows.anchor: وقرأ حمزة: {ليسوءوا} على واحد بالياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the singular reading, the subject may be God or the act of sending, indicated by the earlier mention of sending.
rows.anchor: فاعل يسوء يجوز أن يكون أحد شيئين

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj takes the promise itself as the subject: the promise will sadden their faces.
rows.anchor: وقال الزجاج: ليسوء الوعد وجوهكم

rows.speaker: الكسائي
rows.claim: Al-Kisāʾī reads the verb with first-person plural nūn, attributing the action to God.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الكسائي بالنون (¬2)، وهذا على إسناد الفعل إلى الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tabbara means to perish, while tabbartuhu means I destroyed it; al-Zajjāj also explains breaking and crushing.
rows.anchor: يقال: تبر الشيء يتبر تبارا إذا هلك، وتبره: أهلكه

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Anything broken and crumbled is tabbartuhu; the names for glass and gold fragments derive from this sense.
rows.anchor: قال أبو إسحاق: وكل شيء كسرته وفتته فقد تبرته

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: The commentators, including Qatāda, understand the phrase as destroying and wrecking what the invaders overcame; mā is relative.
rows.anchor: قال المفسرون: أي ليدمروا ويخربوا ما غلبوا عليه

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj reads the phrase temporally: they destroy while in ascendancy, taking mā as a time adverb.
rows.anchor: وقال الزجاج: معناه ليدمروا (¬8) في حال علوهم (¬9)

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Abū ʿAlī prefers the clearer wording that they destroy during their ascendancy, since source mā can function as a time adverb.
rows.anchor: وهو أن يقول: وليتبروا في وقت علوهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God announces that He may show mercy and pardon Israel after taking vengeance on them.
rows.anchor: لعل ربكم أن يرحمكم ويعفو عنكم بعد انتقامه منكم

rows.speaker: المفسرون
rows.claim: The commentators say God returned to them with mercy until they multiplied and spread.
rows.anchor: قال المفسرون: فعاد الله بعائدته ورحمته عليهم حتى كثروا وانتشروا

rows.speaker: الأخفش
rows.claim: Al-Akhfash supplies an omitted condition: God may show mercy if they do good and leave sins.
rows.anchor: قال الأخفش: في الآية محذوف، تقديره: {عسى ربكم أن يرحمكم} إن فعلتم ذلك

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan explains the warning as: if they return to disobedience, God will return to punishment.
rows.anchor: قال الحسن: وإن عدتم بالمعصية عدنا بالعقوبة

rows.speaker: قتادة وإبراهيم
rows.claim: They say Israel returned to evil, so God sent whom He willed to punish them; finally the Arabs imposed lasting subjection and jizya, linked to 7:167.
rows.anchor: قال قتادة وإبراهيم وغيرهم: فعاد (¬6) القوم لشر ما يحضر بهم

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās and the commentators interpret ḥaṣīr as a prison or place of confinement.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس والمفسرون كلهم: سجنا ومحبسا

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Abū Isḥāq derives ḥaṣīr from confinement and illustrates the root through a screened king, joined ribs, and a woven mat.
rows.anchor: حصيرا معناه حبسا؛ من حصرته، أي حبسته فهو محصور

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan instead interprets Hell as a bedding or mattress for the disbelievers, as in 7:41.
rows.anchor: فقال في قوله: {للكافرين حصيرا} أي مهادا وفراشا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The closing statement may begin a general report about all disbelievers' punishment, or continue the account of Israel's punishment for returning to corruption; the address shifts to direct witness.
rows.anchor: فصل يحتمل أن يكون ابتداء إخبار عن الله تعالى في عقاب جميع الكافرين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qurʾān guides to the most just, upright, and sound path; the omitted noun after allatī may be word, path, or state, namely monotheism and Islam.
rows.anchor: أي: يرشد ويدعو للتي، أي إلى التي

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj identifies the best state as God's unity, belief in His messengers, and obedience to Him.
rows.anchor: وقال الزجاج: للحال التي هي أقوم الحالات، وهي توحيد الله والإيمان برسله والعمل بطاعته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The second anna is coordinated with the first: believers are told both of their reward and of the punishment awaiting their enemies.
rows.anchor: فيجب {أن} # للعطف بها على {أن} الأولى

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ says the good tidings cover both clauses, consoling believers harmed by polytheists with news of the unbelievers' punishment.
rows.anchor: قال الفراء: أوقعت (¬1) البشارة على قوله: {أن لهم أجرا} وعلى قوله: {وأن الذين لا يؤمنون}

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ says the written form drops the final wāw of yadʿū although it remains grammatically present; he compares 50:41 and 54:5.
rows.anchor: القياس إثبات الواو في ويدعو، وحذف في المصحف من الكتابة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In anger or impatience, people may pray for harm on themselves, family, or children just as they pray for good.
rows.anchor: أن الإنسان ربما دعا عند الضجر والغضب على نفسه وأهله وولده بما لا يحب

rows.speaker: مجاهد وقتادة
rows.claim: The generic human being rushes to invoke what harms him as quickly as he asks for good; this is the commentators' common explanation.
rows.anchor: هذا قول مجاهد وقتادة وعامة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: In ʿAṭāʾ's transmission, the human is al-Naḍr ibn al-Ḥārith, who made the challenge quoted in 8:32; the good prayer is the believers' request for mercy.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس في رواية عطاء: {ويدع الإنسان} يعني النضر بن الحارث

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās also explains the human's haste as Adam trying to rise before the spirit had fully entered his body.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس في رواية عطاء

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ explains the day as luminous, like the description in 10:67.
rows.anchor: أي: يبصر فيها، فكأن المعنى أنها مضيئة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, day is mubṣir because people can see in it, just as a person may be called mukhbith when his companions are wicked; 17:59 offers a parallel.
rows.anchor: قد أبصر النهار، إذا صار الناس يبصرون فيه فهو مبصر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The day lets people see how to conduct their work; erasing the night-sign makes years countable, as in 10:5.
rows.anchor: وقوله تعالى: {لتبتغوا فضلا من ربكم}، أي: لتبصروا كيف تتصرفون في أعمالكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God made clear everything people need in a way that cannot be confused; Ibn ʿAbbās says this means detailing what was created for benefit.
rows.anchor: وقوله تعالى: {وكل شيء فصلناه}، أي: مما يحتاج إليه

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: In al-Ḥakam's report, Mujāhid says each person's record of misery or felicity is written on a sheet hanging from the neck.
rows.anchor: روى الحكم عن مجاهد قال: مكتوب في ورقة شقي أو سعيد معلقة في عنقه

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan takes the bird fastened to the neck as a person's misery and felicity.
rows.anchor: وهذا كما روي عن الحسن في قوله: {طائره في عنقه} قال: شقاوته وسعادته

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid says the bird means one's deeds, whether they bring misery or felicity.
rows.anchor: وروى ابن أبي نجيح عن مجاهد قال: عمله من شقاوة أو سعادة

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddī interprets it as whatever good or evil has been written for the person.
rows.anchor: وقال السدي: ما كتب له من خير أو شر

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says a person's work and allotted fate remain with him wherever he goes.
rows.anchor: وروي عن ابن عباس: أنه قال عمله وما قدر عليه فهو ملازمه أينما كان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Arabs called good or bad fortune a bird because of their augury; the source then names poetry by Ḥassān and Kathīr witnessing the bird/omen idiom, while condemning augury as pre-Islamic falsehood.
rows.anchor: ذريني وعلمي بالأمور وسيرتي ... فما طائري فيها عليك بأخيلا

rows.speaker: الحسن ومجاهد
rows.claim: Their reading ṭayrihi supports interpreting the bird as one's own deed, good or bad.
rows.anchor: قراءة الحسن ومجاهد: (ألزمناه طيره في عنقه)

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ says bird means a person's deeds in Arabic usage.
rows.anchor: قال الفراء: الطائر معناه عندهم العمل

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abū ʿUbayda says ṭāʾir means one's lot, like the Persian bakht, or what falls to someone when property is apportioned; see 7:131.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو عبيدة: الطائر عند العرب الحظ

rows.speaker: الأزهري
rows.claim: Al-Azharī links each person's fate to God's primordial knowledge and writing of obedient and disobedient descendants of Adam.
rows.anchor: قال الأزهري: والأصل في هذا أن الله تعالى لما خلق آدم علم

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Being in the neck expresses attachment, like a necklace that remains on its wearer.
rows.anchor: قال أبو إسحاق: وإنما يقال للشيء اللازم: هذا في عنق فلان

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Abū ʿAlī compares this idiom to assigning or saddling something on someone; the attached poem by al-Aʿshā illustrates the usage.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو علي: وهذا مثل قولهم: طوقتك كذا وقلدتك كذا

rows.speaker: بعض أهل المعاني
rows.claim: Some exegetes say the neck is specified because good deeds adorn like jewelry while bad deeds disfigure like a fetter.
rows.anchor: إنما خص العنق؛ لأن عمله لا يخلو إما أن يكون خيرا يزينه أو شرا يشينه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On Mujāhid's sheet interpretation, the allotted fate is fixed in a sheet hung at the neck but is not visibly observed.
rows.anchor: ما قسم له أثبت في ورقة وعلقت من عنقه، غير أنا لا نشاهد ذلك مرئيا

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan describes two recording angels, one preserving good deeds and one sins; the folded record accompanies the person in the grave and is brought out at resurrection.
rows.anchor: بسطت لك صحيفة، ووكل بك ملكان، فهما عن يمينك وعن شمالك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The record may be brought out from the person's grave, or the verb may mean that God reveals it after it was unseen in worldly life.
rows.anchor: فعلى هذا معنى: {ونخرج له}، أي: من قبره معه

rows.speaker: يعقوب
rows.claim: Yaʿqūb reads the verb passively; the person's bird, meaning his deed, is brought out as a record entered in the comprehensive book of 18:49.
rows.anchor: وقرأ يعقوب: (ويخرج له يوم القيامة كتابا)

rows.speaker: أبو جعفر
rows.claim: Abū Jaʿfar has the same reading and takes the deed-record as a scroll spread open, as in 81:10.
rows.anchor: وعلى هذا المعنى قرأ أبو جعفر (¬2): (ويخرج له يوم القيامة كتابا)

rows.speaker: ابن عامر
rows.claim: Ibn ʿĀmir reads yulaqqāhu, meaning the person is met with the record; the wording is a causative form, as in 76:11.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن عامر: (يلقاه) (¬4) من قولهم: لقيت فلانا

rows.speaker: الفراء والكسائي
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ and al-Kisāʾī supply an omitted yaqulu, 'it is said/read,' comparing 40:46 and 3:106.
rows.anchor: قال الفراء والكسائي: (يقال) هاهنا مضمرة

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan says everyone will read the record, whether literate or illiterate.
rows.anchor: قال الحسن يقرأه أميا كان (¬3) أو غير أمي

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda says even someone who could not read in life will read on that day.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة: سيقرأ يومئذ من لم يكن قارئا

rows.speaker: بكر بن عبد الله
rows.claim: A believer's good deeds appear on the outside of the record and are envied; after fearing his inner list of sins is ruinous, he is told they were forgiven and recites 69:19.
rows.anchor: يؤتى المؤمن يوم القيامة صحيفة حسناته في ظهره يغبطه الناس عليها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḥasīb means accountant, as in the related description of God in 33:39.
rows.anchor: الحسيب بمعنى الحاسب، كالشريك والنديم

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan calls it God's justice that He makes a person account for himself.
rows.anchor: قال الحسن: عدل والله عليك، من جعلك حسيب نفسك

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddī says the unbeliever asks to audit himself because God declared He is not unjust to servants, then is told to read his book.
rows.anchor: وقال السدي: يقول الكافر يومئذ: إنك قضيت أنك لست بظلام للعبيد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reward of guidance benefits the guided person, while the punishment of misguidance falls on the person who strays.
rows.anchor: ثواب اهتدائه له ولنفسه؛ يعني الخير باهتدائه

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: In ʿAṭāʾ's report, al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīra claimed people should follow him and he would carry their sins.
rows.anchor: قال عطاء عن ابن عباس: يريد أن الوليد بن المغيرة قال: اتبعوني وأنا أحمل أوزاركم

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda insists God neither loads one servant with another's sin nor holds anyone accountable except for his own deeds.
rows.anchor: قال قتادة: لا والله، ما يحمل الله على عبد ذنب غيره

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Abū Isḥāq gives two implications: no one is punished for another's sin and no other bears one's sin; people also must not excuse their own wrongdoing by following others, as in 43:23.
rows.anchor: وفي تأويل هذه الآية وجهان؛ أحدهما: أن الآثم والمذنب لا يؤاخذ بذنب غيره

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās explains that the messenger establishes proof against God's creatures.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: يريد اتخاذ الحجة على خلقه

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda says punishment waits until a divine message and proof have reached the person.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة: إن الله ليس معذبا أحدا حتى يسبق من الله إليه خبر

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Abū Isḥāq says the messenger clarifies what leads to punishment and what earns Paradise.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو إسحاق: أي حتى (¬7) نبين ما به نعذب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This proves obligations arise through revealed law rather than unaided reason: before a messenger's mission, no duty or liability is established.
rows.anchor: وهذا يدل على أن الواجبات إنما تجب بالشرع لا بالعقل

rows.speaker: الشافعي
rows.claim: Al-Shāfiʿī requires inviting people to Islam before battle; Muslims who attack a people unreached by the call are liable for their blood.
rows.anchor: كذلك قال الشافعي -رضي الله عنه-

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: One interpretation is that God commanded the prosperous leaders to obey, but they disobeyed; the omitted object is obedience, and leaders are singled out because others follow them.
rows.anchor: أحدهما: أنهم أمروا بالطاعة فعصوا، وهذا قول سعيد بن جبير

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid, in ʿAbd al-Karīm's report, reads amarnā as 'We increased their number,' meaning their corrupt people multiplied.
rows.anchor: وهو قول مجاهد في رواية عبد الكريم

rows.speaker: سماك وعكرمة وسعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: Other transmissions support the sense 'multiply'; Arab usage includes amara/āmara for becoming or making numerous, with parallel verb forms.
rows.anchor: ونحوه روى # سماك (¬1) عن عكرمة وعمر بن ثابت

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abū ʿUbayda cites the Prophetic expression 'a prolific mare' as linguistic evidence for the abundance sense; Abū Zayd says it means many offspring.
rows.anchor: قال أبو عبيدة (¬1): وقد وجدنا تثبيتا لهذه اللغة

rows.speaker: قوم
rows.claim: Some reject using the phrase as evidence for 'commanded abundance': they parse maʾmūra as rhythmic pairing with maʾbūra, like paired words for mornings and evenings.
rows.anchor: وأبى قوم أن يكون (أمر) بمعنى أكثر

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو
rows.claim: Abū ʿAmr is reported to read amarnā with a doubled mīm; Ibn ʿAbbās' transmitted explanation is that God empowered their wicked people, who rebelled.
rows.anchor: وروى أبو العباس (¬1) -ختن ليث- عن أبي عمرو أنه قرأ {أمرنا} بالتشديد

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Abū Isḥāq interprets the wording as giving them authority; in ʿAṭāʾ's report it means empowering their kings.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو إسحاق: أي جعلنا لهم إمرة وسلطانا

rows.speaker: أبو علي الفارسي
rows.claim: Abū ʿAlī rejects taking the light reading as 'appointed many rulers' and instead compares it to āmarnā, 'increased them,' since a town would not have many chief rulers.
rows.anchor: لا يحمل أمرنا على أن المعنى: جعلناهم أمراء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author says Abū ʿAlī's objection does not refute Ibn ʿAbbās: a town can have many subordinate emirs beneath one chief.
rows.anchor: وهذا الذي قاله أبو علي لا يقدح في قول ابن عباس

rows.speaker: يونس عن أبي عمرو
rows.claim: Yūnus reports Abū ʿAmr's view that the unlengthened light reading cannot mean 'We multiplied'; for that sense he doubled mīm, with only one alif written in the codex.
rows.anchor: أن يونس روى عن أبي عمرو أنه قال: لا يكون أمرنا مخففة بمعنى كثرنا

rows.speaker: ابن كثير
rows.claim: Ibn Kathīr, through Ḥammād ibn Salama, reads āmarnā with a long alif, the prominent dialect for making a people numerous.
rows.anchor: وروى حماد بن سلمة عن ابن كثير: آمرنا بالمد

rows.speaker: نافع
rows.claim: Khārija transmits a similar long-vowel reading from Nāfiʿ.
rows.anchor: ونحو هذا روى خارجة (¬6) عن نافع (¬7)

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Abū Isḥāq offers another sense: increasing the leaders' wealth and means.
rows.anchor: قال أبو إسحاق: ويكون لقوله (¬8): {أمرنا مترفيها} معنى آخر غير كثرة العدد

rows.speaker: أبو عبيد
rows.claim: Abū ʿUbayd favors the common reading because it can bear both command and abundance; mutraf means one made prosperous and spoiled, while commentators gloss it as tyrants, rulers, and kings.
rows.anchor: قال أبو عبيد: الوجه قراءة العامة؛ لاحتماله معنى الأمر والكثرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fusuq here means extreme departure into disbelief; Ibn ʿAbbās says the city thereby deserved punishment.
rows.anchor: وقوله تعالى: {ففسقوا فيها} أي تمردوا في كفرهم

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās glosses the decree taking effect as the city having incurred punishment, linked to 17:15, 28:59, and 11:117.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: يريد استوجبت العذاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God does not destroy a town until its people disobey His command; then the decree of punishment takes effect.
rows.anchor: فقد قال -عز وجل- وحكم بأنه لا يهلك قرية حتى يخالفوا أمره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dammarnā means total destruction; this repeats the preceding point that punishment follows people's violation of God's command.
rows.anchor: أي: أهلكناها إهلاك الاستئصال، والدمار هلاك بالاستئصال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The history of destroyed generations after Noah warns Meccan unbelievers, paralleling 6:6.
rows.anchor: ثم ذكر سنته في إهلاك القرون الماضية تخويفا لكفار مكة

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ says the bāʾ may enter a nominative subject in praise or blame constructions such as 'enough for you' and 'excellent'; it is not allowed with ordinary actions.
rows.anchor: قال الفراء: لو ألقيت الباء كان الحرف مرفوعا

rows.speaker: المفسرون
rows.claim: Al-ʿājila is the present world, contrasted with the delayed Hereafter; worldly seekers receive only the amount God chooses for whom He chooses, not whatever they desire.
rows.anchor: قال المفسرون: أى الدنيا (¬2)، والعاجلة نقيض الآجلة؛ وهي الدنيا عجلت وكانت قبل الآخرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This rebukes those who serve or profess Islam for worldly gain: many seeking it may fail, and whoever gets it receives only a divine allotment before entering Hell.
rows.anchor: هذا ذم لمن أراد بعمله وطاعته وإسلامه الدنيا ومنفعتها وعروضها

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās glosses mazmūm as blameworthy and madḥūr as expelled or driven away.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: ملوما (¬5)، {مدحورا}: منفيا مطرودا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse parallels 3:145 about receiving a share of worldly reward.
rows.anchor: ومعنى هذه الآية كقوله: {ومن يرد ثواب الدنيا نؤته منها}

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Abū Isḥāq says such a person is put in Hell because he did not seek God through his deeds; madḥūr also means removed from God's mercy.
rows.anchor: قال أبو إسحاق: {ثم جعلنا له جهنم}؛ لأنه لم يرد الله بعمله

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās understands the Hereafter as Paradise; the commentators also relate the phrase to seeking the reward or good of the Hereafter, as in 3:145.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: يعني الجنة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Striving for the Hereafter means carrying out God's obligations and fulfilling His rights.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: يريد العمل بفرائض الله والقيام بحقوقه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The striving is accepted only with faith, since God accepts no good deed except from a believer; gratitude means multiplying good deeds, erasing sins, and raising ranks.
rows.anchor: فإن الله لا يقبل حسنة إلا من مصدق

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: God supplies both those seeking the present world and those seeking the Hereafter, giving worldly provision to righteous and wicked alike.
rows.anchor: قال الحسن: كلا نعطي من الدنيا البر والفاجر

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda says the world is divided among good and wicked, while the Hereafter is reserved for the God-fearing.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة: إن الله قسم الدنيا بين البر والفاجر

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Abū Isḥāq says God gives and provides for both Muslim and unbeliever.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو إسحاق: أعلم الله أنه يعطي المسلم والكافر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Maḥẓūr means withheld or forbidden; the root describes blocking someone from something.
rows.anchor: وقوله تعالى: {وما كان عطاء ربك محظورا}، أي: ممنوعا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Worldly preference refers to unequal provision: some people have little, much, ease, or constraint.
rows.anchor: يعني: في الرزق؛ فمن مقل ومن مكثر، ومن موسع عليه ومقتر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One possible reading is that believers' ranks in Paradise differ more than people's worldly provision; the commentators favor this interpretation.
rows.anchor: أحدهما: أن هذا خاص في المؤمنين الذين يدخلون الجنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, the comparison is between believers entering Paradise and unbelievers entering Hell, without asserting differing ranks among believers.
rows.anchor: والثاني: أن هذا التفصيل بين المؤمنين والكافرين

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās supports the first interpretation: Paradise residents divide dwellings and ranks according to their deeds.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: إذا دخلوا الجنان اقتسموا المنازل والدرجات

rows.speaker: المفسرون
rows.claim: The warning is addressed to the Prophet but applies generally to all legally responsible people; alternatively, it addresses every human, as in 65:1.
rows.anchor: المفسرون على أن هذا خطاب للنبي -صلى الله عليه وسلم-، والمعنى عام لجميع المكلفين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fa-taqʿuda is subjunctive after the prohibitive fa with an implied an; the consequence is that associating another god leaves one disgraced and unsupported.
rows.anchor: وقوله تعالى: {فتقعد} انتصب؛ لأنه وقع بعد الفاء جوابا للنهي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Makh dhūl means abandoned, with no protector or helper; the grammar calls the clause a response because the second event results from the first.
rows.anchor: والمخذول: الذي لا عاصم له ولا ناصر

rows.speaker: ابن عباس ومجاهد والحسن وقتادة وابن زيد
rows.claim: The majority of exegetes and linguists interpret qaḍā as 'commanded'; al-Farrāʾ and al-Zajjāj explain it as a decisive, binding command.
rows.anchor: وهو قول مجاهد والحسن وقتادة وابن زيد وعامة المفسرين

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: In a report from Maymūn ibn Mihrān, Ibn ʿAbbās says the wording was wa-waṣṣā rabbuka, with one waw assimilated; otherwise, if it meant decreed, no one could disobey. ʿAlī and ʿAbd Allāh are also said to read it this way.
rows.anchor: وروى ميمون بن مهران عن ابن عباس في هذه الآية، قال: إنما هو (ووصى ربك)

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj takes 'kindness to parents' as another command; Arabic can omit an and put the following noun in the accusative, with a poem as evidence.
rows.anchor: قال الزجاج: أي: وأمر بالوالدين إحسانا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Iḥsānan is governed by an implied command or recommendation, while the preposition bi- belongs with iḥsān and is fronted.
rows.anchor: فعلى هذا ينصب إحسانا بمضمر دل عليه الكلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the common reading, aḥaduhumā is raised by yablughanna and kilāhumā is coordinated with it.
rows.anchor: يرفع {أحدهما} ب {يبلغن}، و {كلاهما} عطف عليه

rows.speaker: حمزة والكسائي
rows.claim: They read yablughāni in the dual; al-Farrāʾ says the verb reflects the previously mentioned two parents, and the following phrase is a new parenthetical clause, as at 5:71 and 21:3.
rows.anchor: وقرأ حمزة والكسائي: (يبلغان)

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: On the dual reading, Abū ʿAlī takes 'one or both' as emphasis referring back to the dual, not as the subject of the verb.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو علي: من قرأ: (يبلغان) جعل قوله: {أحدهما أو كلاهما} معادا على التأكيد

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Abū Isḥāq parses aḥaduhumā as apposition to the dual alif and explains imā as conditional in origin, with jussive marking obscured by the emphatic nūn; compare 2:106, 2:96, and 10:89.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو إسحاق: من قرأ (يبلغان) [يكون {أحدهما أو كلاهما} بدلا من الألف

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Kilā is a singular noun meaning two, restricted to confirming a pair and always annexed; its verbal agreement can be singular or semantic plural, like kull, with examples in 19:95, 18:33, 12:39, 11:114, and 73:20.
rows.anchor: وأما قوله: {كلاهما} فإن كلا اسم مفرد يفيد

rows.speaker: أبو الهيثم وأبو الفتح وأبو علي
rows.claim: Grammarians use poetic examples to show kilā is formally singular, including Labīd's line about both sides of a passage; pronouns may follow form or meaning.
rows.anchor: وقال لبيد: فغدت كلا الفرجين تحسب أنه

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid says reaching old age here includes parents becoming incontinent; al-kibar is the verbal noun of growing old.
rows.anchor: قال مجاهد في قوله: {إما يبلغن عندك الكبر} قال: يخريان ويبولان

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Abū Isḥāq lists seven vocalized and inflected forms of uff; the variants reflect an indeclinable sound-word, case, tanwīn, and the surrounding vowels.
rows.anchor: قال أبو إسحاق: فيه سبع لغات؛ الكسر بغير تنوين وبتنوين

rows.speaker: الأخفش
rows.claim: The common form afī is as though the speaker attributes the complaint to himself: 'my saying this.'
rows.anchor: قال الأخفش: كأنه أضاف هذا القول إلى نفسه

rows.speaker: ابن الأنباري
rows.claim: Ibn al-Anbārī adds forms such as if lak and uffa lak, explaining their case by vocative, prepositional, sound-word, or particle analogies and citing Ḥassān, Abū Ḥayya, and other verse.
rows.anchor: وزاد ابن الأنباري لغات ثلاثا فقال: و (إف لك) بكسر الألف

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ says taʾaffuf is repeatedly saying uff when bothered by a smell.
rows.anchor: وقال الفراء: العرب تقول: جعل فلان يتأفف من ريح وجدها

rows.speaker: الأصمعي
rows.claim: Al-Aṣmaʿī says af is ear dirt and taf is nail dirt, initially expressions of disgust later broadened to any annoyance.
rows.anchor: وقال الأصمعي: الأف: وسخ الأذن، والتف: وسخ الأظفار

rows.speaker: غيره
rows.claim: Another view takes af to mean something little and taf as its paired follow-up, from afaf, a small thing.
rows.anchor: وقال غيره: أف معناه: قلة، وتف إتباع

rows.speaker: ابن الأعرابي
rows.claim: Ibn al-Aʿrābī explains afaf as irritation or impatience.
rows.anchor: وروى ثعلب عن ابن الأعرابي: الأفف: الضجر

rows.speaker: ابن قتيبة
rows.claim: Ibn Qutayba says not to regard any part of caring for one's parents as burdensome or unwelcome.
rows.anchor: وقال القتيبي في قوله: {فلا تقل لهما أف} [أي لا تستثقل شيئا من أمرهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The expression originated in blowing away dust or ash, then came to mean anything one finds burdensome.
rows.anchor: وأصل هذا نفخك للشيء يسقط عليك من تراب أو رماد

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj says af means stench and prohibits even slight annoyance when parents age; instead, serve them.
rows.anchor: وقال الزجاج: معنى (أف) النتن

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: In ʿAṭāʾ's report, af includes vile responses such as wishing one's parents dead or saying one would be relieved of them; compare Abraham's words in 21:67.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس في رواية عطاء: يريد بالأف الرديء من الكلام

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid says not to be disgusted by parents' bodily needs, since they did not recoil from the child's when young; even an offensive smell is no reason to say af.
rows.anchor: روى ليث عن مجاهد: لا تتقذرهما كما كنت تخرأ وتبول

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Do not shout angrily into the parents' faces.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو إسحاق: لا يكل

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says not to answer parents harshly or with coarseness.
rows.anchor: قال عطاء عن ابن عباس: يريد الجواب والغلظة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās explains honorable speech as gentle and kind speech.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: يريد لينا لطيفا

rows.speaker: ابن جريج
rows.claim: Ibn Jurayj says to use the best words one can find.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن جريج: أحسن ما تجد من القول

rows.speaker: عمرو
rows.claim: ʿAmr says one should not refuse anything the parents want.
rows.anchor: وقال عمرو -رضي الله عنه- أي لا تمتنع من شيء يريدانه

rows.speaker: عطاء
rows.claim: ʿAṭāʾ says not to call the parents by name or nickname; address them as father and mother.
rows.anchor: وقال عطاء: لا تسمهما ولا تكنهما

rows.speaker: سعيد بن المسيب
rows.claim: Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib illustrates honorable speech as a penitent servant speaking to a harsh master.
rows.anchor: فقلت: أصلحك الله، كل ما ذكر الله في القرآن

rows.speaker: عروة بن الزبير
rows.claim: ʿUrwa says to be compliant with parents and not refuse anything they like.
rows.anchor: قال عروة بن # الزبير في هذه الآية: يكون لهما ذلولا

rows.speaker: عطاء
rows.claim: ʿAṭāʾ, from Ibn ʿAbbās, says to comply with every request they make.
rows.anchor: وقال عطاء عن ابن عباس: لا يريدان منك أمرا إلا أجبتهما إليه

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqātil says soften one's side, humble oneself, and not resist; the wing is a metaphor for stillness, abandoning stubbornness, and yielding to parents.
rows.anchor: وقال مقاتل: ألن لهما جانبك واخضع لهما، ولا تستصعب عليهما

rows.speaker: عطاء بن أبي رباح
rows.claim: ʿAṭāʾ ibn Abī Rabāḥ says the image also means not raising one's hand against them, since wing can refer to the hand, as in 28:32.
rows.anchor: وقال عطاء بن أبي رباح في هذه الآية: لا ترفع يدك عليهما

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj explains min al-raḥma as the fullness of one's mercy toward the parents.
rows.anchor: قال الزجاج: أي من مبالغتك في # الرحمة لهما

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda says God has taught and commanded this prayer, so people should follow His instruction and discipline.
rows.anchor: قال قتادة: هكذا علمتم وبهذا أمرتم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pray for mercy corresponding to the parents' mercy in raising the child; mentioning upbringing evokes their compassion and toil, and the comparison modifies an omitted verbal noun.
rows.anchor: والكاف في موضع نصب؛ لأنه نعت مصدر محذوف

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās, through ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥa, says 9:113 was revealed afterward.
rows.anchor: قال علي بن أبي طلحة عن ابن عباس: ثم أنزل الله بعد هذا قوله

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda calls the prayer abrogated and says Muslims should not ask mercy for polytheist parents.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة: قوله: {وقل رب ارحمهما} (منسوخ؛ لا ينبغي للمسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Others limit the prayer to Muslim parents, treating the general wording as particular in application; this exception reading of 9:113 is better than declaring parental prayers abrogated.
rows.anchor: وهذا أحسن من أن يحكم بالنسخ على الدعاء للوالدين بالرحمة

rows.speaker: سفيان
rows.claim: Sufyān hopes a prayer for one's parents after the obligatory prayers suffices, by analogy with the salutation upon the Prophet in 33:56 being fulfilled in tashahhud.
rows.anchor: وقال سفيان، وسئل كم يدعو لوالديه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-aʿlam may mean having more objects of knowledge or having firmer knowledge; both descriptions fit God.
rows.anchor: الأعلم من قولك: فلان أعلم، له معنيان

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: Saʿīd ibn Jubayr says the inward lapse may be an impulsive act toward one's parents without intent to harm; sincere filial intent means it is forgiven.
rows.anchor: قال سعيد بن جبير في قوله: {بما في نفوسكم} هو البادرة تكون من الرجل إلى أبويه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God knows inward filial piety or disobedience: He forgives a lapse when the person does not intend disobedience and remains righteous.
rows.anchor: ربكم أعلم بما تضمرون من البر والعقوق

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās glosses ṣāliḥīn as obedient to God and awwābīn as those who return from sin, abandon divine displeasure, and regret slips.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: يريد طائعين لله

rows.speaker: سعيد بن المسيب
rows.claim: Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib says the awwāb is one who sins, repents, then sins and repents again.
rows.anchor: وقال سعيد بن المسيب: هو الذي يذنب ثم يتوب

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan defines the awwāb as someone who intends God in heart and deed.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن: هو الذي يريد الله بقلبه وعمله

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: Saʿīd ibn Jubayr also says the awwāb returns to what is good.
rows.anchor: وقال سعيد بن جبير: يعني الراجعين إلى الخير

rows.speaker: عبيد بن عمير
rows.claim: ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr identifies those who remember their parents and ask forgiveness for them.
rows.anchor: وقال عبيد بن عمير: الذين يذكرون لأبويهم ويستغفرون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report defines an awwāb as one who asks God to forgive what he did in that gathering.
rows.anchor: وروي أنه قال: الأواب: هو الذي يقول: اللهم اغفر لي

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Abū Isḥāq derives awwāb from returning: turning to God in every command and abandoning every prohibition.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو إسحاق: الأواب: هو الراجع إلى الله سبحانه في كل ما أمر به

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd says God mentions relatives after finishing the parents' rights.
rows.anchor: قال ابن زيد: بدأ الله تعالى بالوالدين، فلما فرغ من الوالدين وحقهما ذكر هؤلاء

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says the verse urges maintaining kinship, since family ties carry a duty of connection; al-Ḥasan gives the same sense.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس: هذه الآية حض على صلة القرابة

rows.speaker: أنس
rows.claim: A Prophetic report from Anas advises zakat as purification, maintaining kin, and fulfilling the rights of the asker, neighbor, poor person, and traveler, while forbidding waste.
rows.anchor: وقد فسر النبي -صلى الله عليه وسلم- هذه الآية فيما روى عنه أنس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tabdhīr linguistically means corrupting wealth and spending extravagantly.
rows.anchor: ومعنى التبذير في اللغة: إفساد المال وإنفاقه في السرف

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masʿūd defines wasteful spending as spending where it is not right.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن مسعود: التبذير: النفقة في غير حق

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid says spending an amount as large as Mount Abū Qubays in obedience to God would not count as waste.
rows.anchor: كنت أطوف مع مجاهد حول الكعبة، فرفع رأسه إلى أبي قبيس (¬2) فقال: لو أن رجلا أنفق مثل هذا

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās identifies spenders outside obedience as the wasteful and says Satan's brothers are his allies.
rows.anchor: أي: المنفقين في غير طاعة الله، قاله ابن عباس

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Abū Isḥāq says they do what Satan prompts them to do.
rows.anchor: قال أبو إسحاق: أي يفعلون ما يسول لهم الشيطان

rows.speaker: أهل المعاني
rows.claim: The people of meanings explain brotherhood as agreeing with Satan's invitation and following his way; another view says they will be paired with him in Hell.
rows.anchor: وقال أهل المعاني: مؤاخاة الشيطان: موافقته فيما دعا إليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling spendthrifts Satan's brothers and then condemning Satan as ungrateful warns believers away from him and implies profligates are ungrateful for God's blessings.
rows.anchor: وفيه أيضا إشارة إلى ذم المبذر؛ حيث أخبر أنه أخو الشيطان

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says Satan is a denier of God's blessings.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس في قوله: {وكان الشيطان لربه كفورا} يريد جاحدا لأنعمه

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd says the pronoun refers to the relatives and needy people just mentioned; al-Zajjāj agrees that it refers to kin, poor, and traveler.
rows.anchor: قال [ابن] (¬4) زيد: أي عن هؤلاء الذين أوصيناك بهم

rows.speaker: الحسن وعكرمة
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan and ʿIkrima understand hoped-for mercy as waiting for provision from God.
rows.anchor: قال الحسن وعكرمة: انتظار رزق من الله يأتيك

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj parses ibtighāʾa as a causal accusative; because that appears to make hoped-for mercy the reason for refusal, he reads the underlying sense as poverty and hardship while awaiting God's help.
rows.anchor: قال الزجاج: وهو نصب؛ لأنه مفعول له

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbī and others report that the Prophet, lacking anything to give poor Companions, would turn away in embarrassment and remain silent; God taught him to answer gently.
rows.anchor: وذكر الكلبي وغيره: أن النبي -صلى الله عليه وسلم- (كان إذا سأله فقراء أصحابه

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj also reports that when asked without having anything, the Prophet would wait for provision and then say, 'May God provide for us and you from His bounty.'
rows.anchor: وقال الزجاج: يروى أن النبي -صلى الله عليه وسلم- كان إذا سئل وليس عنده ما يعطي

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd glosses a gentle answer as kind words such as asking God to provide and bless the person.
rows.anchor: قال ابن زيد: قولا جميلا، رزقك الله وبارك الله فيك

rows.speaker: الكلبي والفراء ومجاهد
rows.claim: Al-Kalbī, al-Farrāʾ, and Mujāhid say the gentle answer may be a kind promise.
rows.anchor: وقال الكلبي: عدهم عدة حسنة (¬5)، وهو قول الفراء ومجاهد

rows.speaker: الكسائي
rows.claim: Al-Kisāʾī defines yassartu lahu al-qawl as making speech soft; another idiom for a well-made, sleek horse supports the sense of gentle, easy words.
rows.anchor: فقال الكسائي: يسرت أيسر له القول، أي لينته

rows.speaker: المفسرون
rows.claim: God widens provision for some and constricts it for others; qadara means constriction, as in 65:7 and 89:16, according to the servants' welfare, as explained in 42:27.
rows.anchor: قال المفسرون: يوسع على من يشاء ويضيق على من يشاء

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says God could have made worldly mountains gold and silver for the Prophet, but withheld the world out of honor and prepared the Hereafter for him.
rows.anchor: وقال عطاء عن ابن عباس في هذه الآية: يريد لو أردت أن أبسط (¬5) عليك الرزق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse was discussed earlier at the end of Sūrat al-Anʿām.
rows.anchor: سبق تفسير هذه # الآية في أواخر سورة الأنعام

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Abū Isḥāq says khaṭʾan means a grave sin, like ithm; the word may be a verbal noun, as in 12:97 and 69:37.
rows.anchor: قال أبو إسحاق: معناه: إثما كبيرا

rows.speaker: ابن عامر
rows.claim: Ibn ʿĀmir reads khaṭaʾan with fatḥa, from akhṭaʾa; it can denote an unintended mistake or the act's being wrong, according to Abū Isḥāq.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن عامر {خطئا} بالفتح

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Abū ʿAlī notes that akhṭaʾa can mean sinned and khaṭiʾa can mean missed the right course, so the reading may match the common sense; he cites 2:286 and poetry.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو علي: قد جاء أخطأ بمعنى خطئ أي أثم

rows.speaker: ابن كثير
rows.claim: Ibn Kathīr reads khaṭāʾ with a long vowel, analyzed as a verbal noun from an unattested khāṭaʾa; Abū ʿAlī calls this derivation remote, and prefers the common reading.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن كثير: (خطاء) مكسور الخاء ممدودا

rows.speaker: المفسرون
rows.claim: The lawful grounds for killing are disbelief after Islam, adultery after marriage, or intentional murder; one killed outside these grounds is wronged, and the heir or, absent an heir, the ruler has authority.
rows.anchor: قال المفسرون (¬6): حقها الذي تقتل به: كفر بعد إسلام، أو زنا بعد إحصان

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says the heir's sulṭān is proof or authority.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: يريد حجة

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid says the heir's authority is the right God gave to execute the killer.
rows.anchor: قال مجاهد: سلطانه: حجته التي جعلت له أن يقتل قاتله

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Ḍaḥḥāk says the heir may execute the killer, pardon him, or accept blood money.
rows.anchor: وقال الضحاك في قوله: {سلطانا} إن شاء قتل، وإن شاء عفا

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: One interpretation of the prohibition on excess is that the heir must not kill someone other than the actual killer.
rows.anchor: فقال ابن عباس: هو أن يقتل غير القاتل

rows.speaker: مجاهد وسعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: Mujāhid and Saʿīd ibn Jubayr define excess as killing two or three people for one victim.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد وسعيد بن جبير: هو أن يقتل بالواحد الاثنين والثلاثة

rows.speaker: طلق بن حبيب
rows.claim: Ṭalq ibn Ḥabīb says excess is mutilating the killer.
rows.anchor: قال طلق بن حبيب (¬2): هو أن يمثل بالقاتل

rows.speaker: الحسن وابن زيد
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan and Ibn Zayd describe the pre-Islamic excess of killing a leading man from the killer's tribe because the actual killer was socially low; the heir must stay within the limit.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن وابن زيد: هو أن لا يرضى بالقاتل إذا كان خسيسا

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: God gives the wronged person's heir authority and support to retaliate; Ibn ʿAbbās reportedly told ʿAlī that Ibn Abī Sufyān would prevail based on this verse.
rows.anchor: وقد روي عن زهدم الجرمي (¬1) عن ابن عباس: أنه قال: قلت لعلي ابن أبي طالب

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan likewise said God's wording about the heir's authority explains why Muʿāwiya prevailed over ʿAlī.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن: والله ما نصر معاوية على علي إلا بقول الله

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid, through al-ʿAlāʾ, says the person who first killed is the transgressor; the prohibition can target that initiator, since the victim is supported by the heir or ruler and the heir's retaliation derives from the victim's claim.
rows.anchor: وروى العلاء (¬5) عن مجاهد في قوله: {فلا يسرف في القتل} قال: المسرف: الذي قتل القتيل الأول

rows.speaker: حمزة والكسائي
rows.claim: Their second-person reading can address the unjust initiator: do not kill wrongfully, for the person killed unjustly will be supported through retaliation.
rows.anchor: وقرأ حمزة والكسائي: (فلا تسرف) بالتاء

rows.speaker: حمزة والكسائي
rows.claim: Alternatively, the second-person command addresses the heir, forbidding retaliation against anyone beyond the killer; the wronged person is supported.
rows.anchor: والآخر: أن يكون الخطاب للولي

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Abū Isḥāq says the unjustly killed person is supported in this world by the killer's execution and in the next by abundant reward, while the killer is punished in Hell.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو إسحاق في قوله: {إنه كان منصورا}

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbī says protecting an orphan's wealth includes managing and investing it for profit.
rows.anchor: قال الكلبي: يعني بالقيام عليه وأن يثمر مال اليتيم بالأرباح

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd says a needy guardian may eat from the orphan's wealth according to customary fairness.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن زيد: يعني الأكل بالمعروف؛ أن تأكل معه إذا احتجت إليه

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: In Mujāhid's report, Ibn ʿAbbās permits necessary fair eating, to be repaid upon ability, with no liability if repayment remains impossible.
rows.anchor: وروى مجاهد عن ابن عباس قال: إن احتاج أكل بالمعروف

rows.speaker: إبراهيم
rows.claim: Ibrāhīm says a guardian may eat fairly even if the orphan's wealth is exhausted.
rows.anchor: وروى الحكم عن إبراهيم قال: يأكل بالمعروف

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda says the initial restriction made guardians avoid any mixing, then 2:220 permitted it by recognizing orphans as brethren.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة: هذه الآية كانت جهدا عليهم؛ لا يخالطوهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The best manner is to preserve the wealth; some add growing it, while others allow a needy guardian to eat from it fairly.
rows.anchor: فمعني {بالتي هي أحسن}: الحالة التي هي أحسن؛ وهو الكف عنه

rows.speaker: أهل المعاني
rows.claim: A covenant includes every contract that secures an obligation, such as marriage, partnership, sale, oath, or treaty; it must be fulfilled without betrayal.
rows.anchor: قال أهل المعاني: كل عقد يقدم للتوثق من الأمر فهو عهد

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Abū Isḥāq says every divine command and prohibition is part of the covenant.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو إسحاق: كل ما أمر الله به ونهى عنه فهو من العهد

rows.speaker: صاحب النظم
rows.claim: One grammatical reading means the covenant is asked about and answered for in the reckoning, with its prepositional complement omitted, as in 16:50 and 27:60.
rows.anchor: أحدهما: أن المعنى: كان مسئولا عنه بالجزاء

rows.speaker: صاحب النظم
rows.claim: Alternatively the covenant itself is questioned to rebuke the breaker, like the buried girl questioned to condemn her killer; 5:116 addresses Jesus while the rebuke is aimed at others.
rows.anchor: والثاني: أن العهد يسأل فيقال: لم (¬6) نقضت، تبكيتا للناقض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fulfill the full measure without shortchanging anyone.
rows.anchor: وقوله تعالى: {وأوفوا الكيل إذا كلتم}، أي: أتموه ولا تبخسوا منه

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan identifies the qistās as a steelyard; Ibn ʿAbbās gives the same view through ʿAṭāʾ.
rows.anchor: قال الحسن: هو القبان

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid says qistās means justice, and identifies the word as Persian.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد: هو العدل، بالرومية

rows.speaker: الليث
rows.claim: Al-Layth calls it the fairest set of scales.
rows.anchor: وقال الليث: هو أقوم الموازين

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Abū Isḥāq says it means a just balance of any kind, including scales for money.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو إسحاق: هو ميزان العدل

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Abū ʿAlī permits both a kasra and a ḍamma on qāf, linking the command with 55:9, 11:85, 11:84, and 83:2 against cheating weights or measures.
rows.anchor: ذكر أبو (¬2) علي جواز (¬3) اللغتين فيه؛ ضم القاف (¬4) وكسرها (¬5)

rows.speaker: عطاء وقتادة
rows.claim: ʿAṭāʾ glosses 'better' as closer to God; Qatāda says it is better in reward and outcome, the better end for one who gives full measure.
rows.anchor: وقوله تعالى: {ذلك خير} قال عطاء: يريد أقرب إلى الله (¬7)، وقال قتادة: يقول: خير ثوابا
